desc: This station involves taking a focused history from the parent of an 18-day-old with prolonged jaundice, pale stools and an earlier cord-stump bleed after vitamin K was declined, then arranging same-day urgent assessment and counselling on vitamin K, the two-vessel cord, hips and safe sleep.
explain:
Cholestasis until proven otherwise

Jaundice beyond 14 days in a term baby needs a split (total and conjugated) bilirubin. Pale putty stools, dark urine and hepatomegaly make cholestasis likely, and biliary atresia must be urgently excluded. Outcomes after Kasai portoenterostomy are best when surgery is done early, ideally before about 8 weeks of age. A GP cannot order a test and wait: Noah needs same-day paediatric or ED assessment whatever the pending results.

The cord bleed and vitamin K deficiency bleeding

Vitamin K is a vitamin that helps blood clot. It is not a vaccine, and newborns are born with low levels. Late VKDB occurs from about 2 to 12 weeks and can occur up to 6 months, with intracranial haemorrhage a major risk. Risk factors include no prophylaxis, exclusive breastfeeding and cholestasis. A cord-stump bleed that was slow to stop in an unprophylaxed, now cholestatic infant may be a warning bleed. The plan is urgent coagulation studies (PT/INR) and IM vitamin K 1 mg without delay, by the GP or the receiving team, without waiting for results.

Why oral vitamin K is not an option here

Oral prophylaxis needs several doses and protects less reliably. Cholestasis impairs absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, and active deficiency may already be present. Clinicians should clearly recommend IM treatment while respecting the parent's autonomy. If the parent declines, explain the risks again, involve the paediatric consultant urgently and document the informed refusal. Do not accept oral drops as a compromise.

Sunlight and jaundice

Sunlight is not a treatment for cholestatic jaundice and is unsafe for newborns because of the risk of sunburn. Phototherapy treats unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and does not address this problem.

Two-vessel cord

A two-vessel cord (single umbilical artery) can be a normal variant, but it raises the chance of an undetected congenital anomaly, especially of the renal tract and the heart. For an isolated finding with a normal antenatal scan and normal newborn examination, renal tract ultrasound is commonly arranged. Cardiac assessment (echocardiogram) is indicated if an anomaly is suspected or the newborn examination is abnormal, not automatically for every isolated two-vessel cord.

Hips

Barlow tests whether a located hip can be dislocated (adduct the flexed hip with gentle backward pressure). Ortolani relocates a dislocated hip (abduct the flexed hip while lifting the greater trochanter forward), felt as a clunk. A positive or abnormal finding needs hip ultrasound and paediatric or orthopaedic review. A cousin or nephew with DDH is a second-degree relationship and not a standard risk factor. With a normal documented hip examination and no first-degree family history, the plan is continued hip checks at routine visits, with ultrasound only if the examination is abnormal or other risk factors (for example first-degree family history or breech presentation) are present.

SUDI, SIDS and safe sleep

SUDI is the umbrella term for sudden unexpected death in infancy and includes SIDS and fatal sleep accidents such as accidental suffocation. SIDS is the sudden unexpected death of a baby under 1 year, usually during sleep, with no cause found after thorough investigation. Risk reduction: sleep on the back with feet at the foot of the cot, face and head uncovered with nothing loose near the head, a cot meeting Australian standards with a firm flat mattress and lightweight tucked-in bedding, a smoke-free environment, the baby's own safe sleep space in the same room as a caregiver for the first 6 to 12 months, and breastfeeding if possible. Sofa sleeping, pillows and tummy sleeping are particular hazards.

Prioritising

With a baby who may have both cholestasis and an active vitamin K deficiency, the urgent referral comes first. Hip, cord and sleep counselling can be brief, with written resources and follow-up for the rest.
focus: Newborn check and parent counselling: vitamin K, hips, jaundice, safe sleep
guide:
A high-performing candidate takes a focused history that finds the pale stools, dark urine and the cord-stump bleed, and asks directly about vitamin K without blame. They recognise that jaundice at 18 days with pale stools and dark urine is cholestasis until proven otherwise, so biliary atresia must be excluded urgently. They also recognise that the cord bleed in an infant with no vitamin K prophylaxis and cholestasis may be a warning bleed of late VKDB. They arrange same-day paediatric or ED assessment by phone and letter without waiting for any result. They ensure coagulation studies (PT/INR) are done with the split bilirubin and recommend IM vitamin K without delay. They explain that oral vitamin K is not an acceptable alternative in this situation. They explain that vitamin K is not a vaccine, respect the parent's autonomy and escalate to the paediatric consultant if the parent declines. They answer the sunshine question clearly. Once the urgent plan is set, they answer the other questions briefly. They explain that a two-vessel cord is often a normal variant but warrants renal tract ultrasound and cardiac review only if indicated. They explain Barlow and Ortolani and that a second-degree relative with DDH does not justify a routine hip ultrasound when the hip examination is normal and there is no first-degree family history. They distinguish SUDI from SIDS, correct the unsafe sleep practices, and close with a summary, written resources and follow-up.

A borderline candidate notes the jaundice but does not link the pale stools, dark urine and cord bleed. They may order a split bilirubin and wait for the result before referring, or send Noah for outpatient bloods. They may offer oral vitamin K drops as a choice. They may order a hip ultrasound because of the sister's baby, or imply an echocardiogram is mandatory for the two-vessel cord. They may spend most of the time on safe sleep and hips, or sound judgemental about the vitamin K decision.
patient:
Profile:

  • Name: Alex Nguyen, parent of Noah (18 days old, firstborn)

  • Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander: No

  • Location: General Practice clinic

  • Demeanour: tired, anxious and a little defensive about the vitamin K decision. You become tearful if blamed.

Opening line: 'Noah is still really yellow. My mum says it's just breastmilk jaundice.'

History (give only if asked):

  • Jaundice: Noticed on day 3. It improved a little but never went away and has looked worse in the last week.

  • Stools: Mustard yellow at first. Since about day 10 they have been getting paler. Now they are pale grey-white, like putty. You have a photo on your phone and show it if asked.

  • Urine: Nappies are dark yellow-brown and stain.

  • Feeding and general: Breastfed 8 times a day with a good latch, many wet nappies. He wakes for feeds, is not floppy or drowsy, and has had no vomiting, fever, fits or unusual irritability. You are not aware of any head injury.

  • Bleeding: Around day 9 the cord stump bled as it was about to fall off. It soaked a cloth and you pressed on it for 10 to 15 minutes before it stopped. The midwife said it was probably normal. No bruises, nosebleeds, bleeding from the mouth, blood in vomit or blood in the nappy. Nothing is bleeding today.

  • Vitamin K: 'We said no to it at the hospital. We thought it was a vaccine and we're not comfortable with vaccines. He had no drops either.' You signed a form. Say this only when asked about vitamin K or injections.

  • Pregnancy and family: Uncomplicated pregnancy. The 20-week scan said the cord has two vessels instead of three, and nobody has mentioned it since. No diabetes, medications, alcohol or drugs. Mother's blood group A positive. No family history of liver disease, bleeding disorders or jaundice in babies. No first-degree family history of hip problems.

  • Sleep (only if asked): Noah sleeps in your bed, or on the couch on a pillow with you when you are exhausted. He is wrapped tightly in a fluffy blanket and sometimes put on his tummy because he settles. His other parent smokes on the balcony.

Cues and questions to ask the candidate (spread through the counselling):

  • 'Is it because we said no to vitamin K? Did we cause this?'

  • 'Do we just need more sunshine?' Accept the answer if the candidate advises against it and explains why. If told sunlight is fine, say 'OK, I'll take him to the park.'

  • 'Can we get the blood test at the lab and wait for the results before going anywhere?' or 'Can we come back tomorrow?' Agree to go today only after a clear explanation of the urgency.

  • 'Is there a drops version of vitamin K instead? Would that be fine?' If the candidate offers drops as acceptable, say 'Good, drops then.' If the candidate clearly recommends the injection and explains why drops are not suitable now, say 'If that is what is safest for him, OK. I would rather the hospital doctors do it.' If the candidate is dismissive or does not explain, say 'I need to think about it' and stay hesitant about the injection, but agree to go to hospital.

  • 'My sister's baby needed a hip brace. Should Noah have a hip scan?'

  • 'The midwife said two vessels in the cord. Does that matter?'

  • 'A friend's baby died last year and they said SUDI, not SIDS. Is that different?' Ask this if the candidate raises sleep, or in the last two minutes.

Use only the script above. Give a realistic answer if asked anything outside it. Interrupt if the candidate uses medical jargon without explaining it.
points: Jaundice beyond 14 days in a term baby, especially with pale stools and dark urine, is cholestasis until proven otherwise. Refer for same-day paediatric or ED assessment, not outpatient tests.
A cord bleed in an infant who had no vitamin K and has cholestasis may be a warning bleed of late VKDB. Get urgent PT/INR and give IM vitamin K without delay.
Vitamin K is not a vaccine. Oral vitamin K is not an acceptable alternative in cholestasis or suspected VKDB, so recommend IM clearly and escalate if the parent declines.
Sunlight is not a treatment for jaundice in newborns.
A two-vessel cord is often a normal variant: arrange renal tract ultrasound, with cardiac review only if an anomaly is suspected or the examination is abnormal.
A normal hip examination with a second-degree relative with DDH means routine hip checks. Order ultrasound only for an abnormal examination or true risk factors.

stem:
You are a GP seeing Noah, an 18-day-old boy, with his parent, Alex Nguyen. Alex has brought Noah in because 'he is still yellow'. A tertiary children's hospital with a paediatric emergency department is 25 minutes away.

The hospital discharge summary (day 2) records: term (39+3 weeks) spontaneous vaginal delivery, cephalic presentation, birth weight 3.4 kg, two-vessel umbilical cord noted at birth, normal newborn examination including hips and heart sounds, newborn screening collected. Vitamin K status is not recorded.

Your examination findings today (already completed):

  • Alert, feeding, normal tone. Temperature 36.8 °C, heart rate 140/min, respiratory rate 40/min, weight 3.7 kg

  • Jaundiced to the thighs. No pallor, bruising or petechiae

  • Cord stump has separated and the umbilicus is dry with no active bleeding

  • Anterior fontanelle soft and flat. Heart sounds normal with no murmur

  • Abdomen soft, liver edge palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin, spleen not palpable

  • Hips: Barlow and Ortolani negative bilaterally, abduction symmetrical

The total time for this station is 11 minutes.
tasks: Take a focused history from the parent (3 minutes).

Explain your assessment and arrange the management Noah needs today. Counsel the parent on their questions: vitamin K, jaundice, the two-vessel cord, hips and safe sleep (8 minutes). Deal with the urgent problem first. The hip, cord and sleep questions can be answered briefly.
